title: How to Get More From GitHub Copilot Without Burning Through Your Credits
excerpt: GitHub Copilot has become a genuinely useful part of how I build software, but using it effectively isn't just about asking it to write more code. I've been learning that how you use AI matters just as much as having access to it.
content:
I've been using GitHub Copilot a lot recently, both at work and on personal projects, and having an AI assistant sitting inside VS Code has become incredibly useful.

It can explain code I don't understand, suggest ways of solving problems, help track down errors and, when I want it to, make changes to the application for me.

But the more I've used it, the more I've realised that getting the most from Copilot takes more than access to the most powerful model and asking it to do as much as possible. There's a bit of a skill to using it well.

That's especially true now that Copilot usage is measured in AI credits. Some things I do with Copilot consume credits, while others, such as the normal code completions that appear as I type, don't. So the way I use the tool can make a surprisingly big difference to how quickly I get through my monthly allowance, and I've started thinking more carefully about what I need Copilot to do.

## Not all Copilot usage is the same

One of the first things I found confusing was the difference between the suggestions that appear while I'm coding and the more substantial AI interactions.

Inline suggestions are probably the part of Copilot most people notice first. I'm typing, Copilot predicts what I might want next, and I accept it with Tab. I might start writing a function and Copilot suggests the rest based on what I'm already doing.

That's very different from opening Copilot Chat and asking it to analyse my application, or asking Agent mode to implement an entire feature.

GitHub's current usage model treats these differently. Code completions and Next Edit suggestions don't consume AI credits, whereas more substantial interactions can, depending on the model and the amount of processing involved.

That's changed how I think about Copilot. I don't need to worry every time I accept an autocomplete suggestion. The things to be conscious of are the larger requests where I'm asking the AI to reason about a problem or do a significant amount of work.

## Agent mode is powerful, but I don't need it for everything

Agent mode is probably one of the most impressive parts of Copilot. Instead of asking a question and then making the changes myself, I can give Copilot a goal and let it investigate the project, work out what needs changing and make the changes across multiple files. Depending on the task, it can also run commands, look at the results and keep going. For a large feature, that's incredibly useful.

The problem is that it's very tempting to use Agent mode for absolutely everything.

If I want to know what a particular function does, I don't need an autonomous coding agent. If I've got an error message I don't understand, I probably don't need one either. Even a small change to a single component doesn't necessarily justify handing the task to an agent.

So I've started using a much simpler rule: use the simplest Copilot feature that can solve the problem. For a question or explanation, I use Chat. For a small code change, I use an edit or a focused request. When I need several related files changed, or want Copilot to work through a larger task, that's when Agent mode earns its cost.

## Plan bigger changes before asking Copilot to build them

Another thing I've found useful is separating planning from implementation.

When I'm working on something fairly complicated, my first instinct used to be to tell Copilot what I wanted and let it get started. That can work, but it can also leave Copilot making a series of assumptions I don't agree with.

Say I want to make a significant change to the article system on my website. Instead of immediately saying, "Build this new system," I can first ask Copilot to look at the existing application and explain how it thinks the change should be implemented, without changing any files. That gives me a chance to look at the proposed approach and correct it before any code has been touched. Once I'm happy with it, I ask Copilot to implement it.

It seems like a small difference, but I think it matters a lot when working with AI. I'm still making the architectural decisions and using Copilot to help implement them, instead of letting it decide what the application should become. It can also save credits, because I'm less likely to end up asking Copilot to undo and redo large chunks of work after an unclear request.

## Give Copilot the context it actually needs

There's a natural assumption that more context is always better for AI. I'm not convinced it is.

If I'm trying to fix a problem with my Articles page, Copilot probably doesn't need to understand every component, database table and page in my application. If the problem is contained in two or three files, giving it those files and a clear description is likely to be more useful than throwing the whole project at it.

This matters even more in Agent mode, because the agent can explore the project and build up a large amount of context as it works. Being explicit about the scope of a task helps enormously.

Instead of saying:

> "Fix the articles."

I can say something like:

> "The Articles page currently displays all articles. Change it so clicking a tag filters the displayed articles. Use the existing Supabase article/tag relationships. Don't change the database schema or the article card component."

That tells Copilot what the problem is, what I want it to do and, importantly, what I don't want it to change, which gives it a much clearer idea of what success looks like.

## Don't let every task become one enormous conversation

Another easy trap is keeping the same conversation going forever.

It might start with a question about the Articles page. Then I ask about Supabase. Then we move on to authentication, some CSS changes and a completely new feature. Before long, I'm talking to Copilot in a conversation that holds the history of half the application, and that history doesn't help.

Now, when I move on to a different piece of work, I start a new conversation. One might be about the Articles page, another about the Supabase admin area and another about building the Mentoring section. It keeps each discussion focused, makes it much easier to understand why Copilot is suggesting what it suggests, and stops the context of an old problem leaking into an unrelated one.

## The most powerful model isn't always the right model

Having access to several AI models brings another temptation: assuming the most capable one is automatically the best choice.

For a difficult architectural problem, a complicated debugging session or a task that needs a lot of reasoning, a more powerful model can make sense. But if I'm asking Copilot to explain a simple JavaScript function, I don't need the most expensive model available.

For straightforward tasks, automatic model selection or a lower-cost model is often the better fit. GitHub's Auto model selection is designed to pick an appropriate model for the task, and GitHub also publishes information about the relative cost of different models.

I've started thinking about models the way I'd think about tools in a workshop. You don't reach for the biggest tool just because you have it. You use the one that suits the job.

## Being specific saves more than just credits

One of the biggest lessons I've taken from using AI is that a good prompt doesn't have to be a long one. What it has to do is remove ambiguity.

If I ask:

> "Make the article page better."

I'm leaving an enormous amount open to interpretation. Better visually? Faster? More accessible? Better on mobile? Different typography? A different layout?

A much better request might be:

> "Improve the spacing and typography on the article page. Keep the existing layout, colours and components. Make the page easier to read on desktop and mobile, but don't change the database or routing."

Now Copilot has some boundaries. That matters because every time it gets something wrong, I have to spend more time explaining what I wanted and possibly ask for more changes. A little more thought before sending the first request can avoid a surprising amount of back-and-forth.

## I still need to be the developer

Perhaps the biggest thing I've learned is that Copilot works best for me when I treat it as an assistant and not a replacement.

I can ask it to do things that would have taken me considerably longer to work out myself. It can explain unfamiliar code, suggest approaches and handle some of the repetitive parts of development. But I still need to understand what I'm asking it to build, review the code it produces, decide whether the architecture makes sense and recognise when its solution isn't what I want.

That last part is especially important, because AI can produce perfectly valid-looking code that solves the wrong problem. Something compiling doesn't mean it's the right solution.

For me, that's one of the most interesting parts of learning to use AI for development. The skill is changing shape. Instead of spending all my time remembering syntax or working out every small implementation detail, I can spend more of it thinking about the problem I'm solving and reviewing the solution I'm given.

## My simple rules for using Copilot

I've ended up with a fairly simple set of rules for myself:

- Use inline suggestions freely, because they speed up the coding I'm already doing.
- Use Chat for explanations and questions, instead of automatically reaching for Agent mode.
- Use Agent mode when I want Copilot to do a substantial piece of work, especially across multiple files.
- For bigger changes, plan first and implement second. I'd rather spend a few minutes discussing an approach than half an hour asking Copilot to undo something it shouldn't have changed.
- Keep the context focused, instead of assuming Copilot needs to know everything about the application.
- Start a new conversation for each new piece of work, especially when it's unrelated to what I was doing before.
- Use the right model for the task, instead of automatically picking the most powerful option.

None of this means I use Copilot less. If anything, I think I use it better.

## The real benefit isn't writing more code

When I first started using Copilot, the obvious attraction was that it could write code for me. That's still useful, of course, but I'm beginning to think it isn't the most interesting part.

The bigger benefit is having something I can talk problems through with. If I don't understand why something is happening, I can ask. If I'm not sure how to approach a problem, I can explore the options. If I've got an idea but don't know how to implement it, I can talk through the implementation. And when I do know what I want, Copilot helps me turn it into working software much faster.

The trick is making sure I'm still driving. AI can make software development faster, but using it well is a skill in itself, and for me that skill comes down to knowing what to ask it to do, when to ask, and when to do the thinking myself.
